strengths: KOCO-BENCH addresses an important and under-served problem: evaluating whether models can acquire and apply knowledge from an explicitly supplied software-domain corpus, rather than merely testing knowledge already encoded in model parameters.
The artifact is substantial and grounded in realistic software ecosystems: 11 framework corpora, 25 projects, 131 core functions, 978 tests, and 107 knowledge questions spanning six emerging domains.

Executable unit and integration tests provide a more objective evaluation of code correctness than similarity metrics or LLM judges. The requirements, environments, and tests reportedly undergo iterative human verification.

The empirical coverage is broad, including ten language models, several training- and retrieval-based specialization methods, coding agents, pass@any evaluation, stronger retrieval and instruction-tuning variants, context-length ablations, error analysis, and cost analysis.

The results consistently establish that these tasks are difficult and that agentic access to repositories and corpora can substantially outperform direct generation, particularly in the RAG-framework domain.
weaknesses: The evidence does not cleanly isolate acquisition or use of domain knowledge. There is no corpus-access ablation for agents, oracle-retrieval condition, random/irrelevant-corpus control, or analysis of whether passed cases actually depend on corpus knowledge. The reported differences may therefore reflect general repository exploration, execution feedback, model strength, or retrieval quality.

The benchmark's advertised multi-granularity evaluation is only partially substantiated. Quantitative experiments primarily evaluate function-body generation; project-level generation is a qualitative case study on one framework with unspecified sample size and manual runtime fixes. Domain knowledge understanding is evaluated only for the two domains without code-generation projects, confounding task type with domain.

Benchmark validation is insufficiently documented. The paper does not report test coverage values, mutation testing, independent reimplementation checks, annotation agreement, Q&A acceptance/revision rates, or per-project sample counts. Filtering questions based on failures of three small models establishes difficulty but not validity or representativeness.

Several prominent conclusions substantially exceed the evidence. The corpus-size claim is inferred from only a few heterogeneous domain-level points and is confounded by framework and task difficulty. The catastrophic-forgetting claim is based on one small aggregate table without named framework pairs, training order, repeated runs, variance, or replay/joint-training controls; it cannot support the claim that semantic distance largely determines forgetting.

Baseline comparisons are difficult to interpret. SFT and LoRA use raw next-token training, while RAG uses only top-5 BM25 results queried by function names and signatures. These limited configurations do not justify broad claims about existing domain-specialization methods. No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run analyses are reported despite small and uneven task sets.

The agent comparison remains heavily resource-confounded even after matching the base model: Claude Code consumes roughly 620k tokens per sample versus about 26k for the open-source agents, and exact prompts, software versions, and comparable budget controls are absent.

Contamination and reproducibility assurances are incomplete. Public frameworks and projects could have entered later models' training data; the contamination detector is described only at a high level and its reported aggregate scores lack calibration. The manuscript promises a public release but displays no usable repository link, and exact repository commits, complete prompts, seeds, and API snapshots are not specified. These concerns currently prevent a clear Findings recommendation, although the benchmark could become suitable after stronger validation, controlled ablations, and moderated claims.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: evaluating whether models can acquire and apply unfamiliar framework knowledge, rather than merely testing knowledge already present in model parameters.

Pairing explicit knowledge corpora with executable code-generation tasks is a useful benchmark design direction. The use of real frameworks and projects, Docker environments, unit tests, integration tests, and both strict Pass@1 and partial test-pass metrics could support more realistic evaluation than similarity-based scoring.

The benchmark covers multiple types of domain knowledge and includes several baseline families—parameter updating, retrieval, nearest-neighbor methods, and coding agents. The additional dense-retrieval, instruction-tuning, context-length, Pass@any, and same-base-model agent experiments address some natural questions.

The distinction between function-, module-, and project-level specifications is potentially valuable, and the manuscript is generally organized clearly enough to understand the intended benchmark and experimental workflow.

The low absolute results and the strong Claude Code result on the otherwise-zero RAG subset provide some evidence that at least part of the benchmark is difficult without effective knowledge access yet remains solvable.
weaknesses: The benchmark is too small and uneven to support several broad conclusions: it contains only 131 core functions and 107 questions, code generation covers only four domains, and knowledge QA is evaluated on two different domains. Some reported percentages therefore correspond to very few examples, but the paper provides no confidence intervals, significance tests, or sensitivity analysis. Small differences described as meaningful improvements or regressions may amount to one or two tasks.

The central claim that the benchmark evaluates knowledge acquisition is not cleanly isolated. Inference methods receive both the framework corpus and project context, while the projects themselves may contain redundant implementations, usage patterns, or near-duplicates of the target logic. The paper reports no overlap or clone analysis between corpora, project contexts, target functions, tests, and other projects, and provides no controlled comparison separating framework knowledge from repository-context information.

Benchmark validity is insufficiently established. Requirements and tests are partly agent-generated, yet there is no quantitative human-validation study, inter-annotator agreement, ambiguity rate, mutation-testing analysis, held-out manual audit, or evidence that the tests reject plausible incorrect implementations. Branch coverage and passing the reference implementation do not by themselves establish semantic adequacy. Similar validation is missing for the automatically generated multiple-choice questions and distractors.

The advertised multi-granularity contribution is not convincingly evaluated. Main experiments concern function-body generation. Project-level generation receives only an anecdotal qualitative analysis with an unclear number of projects or trials, and generated code is manually repaired until execution succeeds. No reproducible project-level success metric is reported, and module-level generation is not evaluated.

The conclusion that existing domain-specialization methods provide only marginal gains is much broader than the evidence. Most comparisons use a single 7B base model; SFT is raw next-token training over randomly concatenated files; and the primary RAG baseline uses BM25 with queries limited to function names and signatures. These are weak implementations relative to modern code retrieval, reranking, context construction, or agentic retrieval, so their failure does not establish a general limitation of domain specialization.

Several secondary claims are not supported by rigorous analyses. The corpus-size plot appears to compare only a handful of domains/frameworks while confounding corpus size with domain, task difficulty, corpus composition, and sample count; it cannot show that more data hinders learning. The continual-learning result lacks framework identities, training order, repeated runs, variance, matched-data controls, and joint-training or replay baselines, so the drop cannot justify claims that semantic distance determines catastrophic forgetting.

The agent comparison remains strongly confounded by implementation, tool affordances, budgets, and cost. Claude Code consumes roughly 620k tokens per sample versus about 26k for the open-source agents. Using Claude as the base model for all systems reduces one confound but does not make the systems or compute budgets comparable, so conclusions about an open-versus-closed agent gap should be qualified.

Contamination control is not convincing. Several evaluated models have cutoff dates after the selected frameworks were created, and release date is substituted for unknown training cutoff for some models. A single unexplained contamination-index method and low observed task performance cannot rule out exposure to framework code or documentation. Exact repository commits, collection dates, and temporal relationships are needed.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate from the manuscript alone. The promised release URL is missing, and the paper does not identify exact framework/project commits, dataset splits, prompts, retrieved chunks, model/API versions and access dates, hardware, random seeds, per-domain training sizes, or complete evaluation procedures. Referring to official implementations and default configurations is insufficient, especially for adapted methods and proprietary agents.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies and omissions: tables described as spanning six domains actually evaluate code generation on four; aggregation and weighting across differently sized domains are not explained; the error analysis omits its sample size, annotation protocol, and agreement; and the comparison to prior benchmarks is largely a feature checklist rather than an empirical demonstration of added validity. Overall, the benchmark premise is promising, but substantial validation, controlled experimentation, and release documentation are required before it meets the soundness and reproducibility threshold for Findings.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely evaluation gap: measuring whether LLMs can acquire and apply an explicitly supplied software-domain knowledge corpus, rather than merely testing knowledge already encoded during pretraining.

KOCO-BENCH has a thoughtful, practically motivated design that pairs documentation, source code, and examples with objectively evaluated code-generation and knowledge-understanding tasks. Executable unit and integration tests are substantially more reliable than similarity metrics or LLM judges.

The construction effort is substantial: 11 frameworks, 25 real projects, 131 core functions, 978 tests, Docker environments, multi-level requirements, branch-oriented test construction, and human review of agent-assisted annotations.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering open and closed LLMs, SFT, LoRA, sparse and dense RAG, kNN-based approaches, instruction-tuned training, and multiple coding agents. The controlled Claude-Sonnet experiments partly disentangle agent scaffolding from base-model capability.

Useful supplementary analyses address sequence length, Pass@any, cost, contamination, and concrete failure modes. The API-misuse and data-constraint case studies help establish why the benchmark is difficult.
The benchmark is highly relevant to code-oriented NLP and has plausible community value. The central descriptive result—that current methods and models struggle on these tasks—is generally supported.
weaknesses: The paper advertises evaluation from function-level through project-level generation, but the quantitative experiments primarily cover only 131 core functions. Project-level generation is represented by a qualitative experiment on one framework with manual debugging, so the broad multi-granularity claim is not yet convincingly validated.

Coverage is uneven and partly disjoint: code generation is evaluated in four domains, whereas knowledge understanding is evaluated only in Embodied AI and the Ascend ecosystem. Consequently, the benchmark does not directly measure whether improved knowledge understanding predicts improved code application within the same frameworks.

Several strong analytical conclusions exceed the evidence. The corpus-size claim appears to compare only a small number of heterogeneous frameworks without correlation statistics or controls for task difficulty. The catastrophic-forgetting claim is based on a compact aggregate table without reporting framework pairs, training order, variance, repeated runs, or suitable joint-training controls.

The evaluation reports point estimates without confidence intervals, significance tests, or variation across random seeds. Given the small per-domain sample sizes—visible from the coarse score increments—some method differences may correspond to only one or two functions.

Test validity needs stronger empirical auditing. Branch coverage and agreement with the reference implementation do not establish resistance to incorrect implementations; mutation testing, estimates of false acceptance/rejection, and independent manual inspection of a sample would better support the claim of rigorous evaluation. Call-sequence checks may also favor the reference implementation over alternative correct solutions.

The contamination analysis is underspecified: it is unclear which model produces each reported index, and a low detection score cannot establish that the benchmark is contamination-free. This is especially relevant for models whose training cutoffs or release dates postdate some selected frameworks and projects.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete for a benchmark paper. The manuscript does not provide an accessible release location, complete prompts, seeds, hardware/training budgets, precise corpus snapshots and project commits, annotation-agreement statistics, or sufficiently detailed adaptations of kNN-LM, kNM-LM, and DSCC. Reproducing closed-model and Claude Code results may also be difficult as these systems evolve.

Overall, this is a sound and potentially influential benchmark contribution, but the limited validation of project-level evaluation and the overextended scaling and forgetting claims prevent a clear main-conference recommendation in its current form. Narrowing those claims and strengthening statistical and artifact validation could move it to Conference.
